content:
Hi! A student of mine (@Noé Guillemoles) is working on implementing and verifying Gaussian elimination. As part of this project, he built API for an efficient representation of docs#Matrix based on docs#Vector. My feeling is this deserves to be contributed to batteries, is that correct?

@Bhavik Mehta I assume you already have some similar code for your numerics projects, do you have plans to upstream it somewhere?
I don't actually, though I think @Paul Cadman might have relevant things
Batteries is a good place for that. Does it handle sparse matrices?
No, but this would be a different type in any case, right?
Ah, do you mean the Gaussian elimination proces? The answer is also no for now.
Why would this go in Batteries? Let's not try to turn Batteries into a computer algebra library. This should be a discussion for #Computer algebra > .

Sorry, my original message was maybe a bit ambiguous, for now I'm talking about contributing the basic API for matrices, not the Gaussian elimination (yet). Do you think even the data structure should be somewhere else?

@Kim Morrison The matrix data type, basic operations and lemmas is fine for Batteries.

@Anatole Dedecker Not necessarily, this is the type I think is best:

structure Matrix (m n : Nat) (a : Type _) where
  data : Array a
  get : Fin m -> Fin n -> a

Then various specialized constructors mkDense, mkSparse, mkDiag, etc.

It would seem more natural to me to have a MatrixLike typeclass for the common API. For example, I claim that, for Gaussian elimination of sparse matrices, you really want to use the fact that they are sparse to optimize the algorithm (e.g completely skipping the zero coefficients in a column).
Also, how does this allow updating the matrix? And what if the natural way I want to represent my sparse matrix uses multiple arrays instead of one?
I think it's more important to have matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication without worrying whether the matrix is dense, sparse, diagonal,...
In the end, it's the implementer that decides.

François G. Dorais said:

Kim Morrison The matrix data type, basic operations and lemmas is fine for Batteries.

Anatole Dedecker Not necessarily, this is the type I think is best:

structure Matrix (m n : Nat) (a : Type _) where
  data : Array a
  get : Fin m -> Fin n -> a

Then various specialized constructors mkDense, mkSparse, mkDiag, etc.

If you want it to be efficient storing a closure in a structure is definitely not the way to go

François G. Dorais said:

I think it's more important to have matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication without worrying whether the matrix is dense, sparse, diagonal,...

But presumably you want a different implementation for multiplication of sparse matrices, no? I'm not very familiar with all of this to be fair, but I thought you also gain time complexity by working with sparse matrices.
In any case, what your student has done is what matters. Even just having dense matrices would be more than what currently exists.
There's an argument to be made that efficient matrices could be built on top of mathlib, with a * b = ofMathlib (a.toMathlib * b.toMathlib), but maybe this allocates too many intermediate closures
Optimistically those closures could be eliminated with suitable inline attributes in mathlib

If you want the best code possible your code for accessing the matrix has to use Array.get or uget in a fashion that is directly visible to the compiler. It has special knowledge about the lifetime properties of objects stored in arrays.
For example running a[i] + b[i] never needs to reference count if a and b remain live (such as in a loop)
"directly visible" includes things seen through some form of inline?

Well, for one, when using mathlib matrix multiplication, the Fintype requirement corresponds to allocating a range list of indices 0, ..., n-1. There are certainly more efficient ways to multiply matrices...

Eric Wieser said:

"directly visible" includes things seen through some form of inline?

After inlining and specialization there should be full applications of Array.get

François G. Dorais said:

In any case, what your student has done is what matters. Even just having dense matrices would be more than what currently exists.

Thanks! For additional context, Noé is a first-year undergraduate student (and I'm more of a mathematician than a computer scientist), so it is completely possible that the code is not general or efficient enough. But "basic API for dense matrices" sounded like something relatively easy to contribute, and a nice way for him to get suggestions from CS-oriented people.

Robin Arnez said:

Well, for one, when using mathlib matrix multiplication, the Fintype requirement corresponds to allocating a range list of indices 0, ..., n-1. There are certainly more efficient ways to multiply matrices...

I guess this also forces you to use well-behaved numerics that are associative, so not float.
Haha yeah yesterday I accidentally instantiated Fintype UInt64 and I was wondering why was my computer freezing.

Anyway, I'm working on basic library for n-dimensional arrays with bindings to BLAS. It is really an abstract layer between the implementation and the mathematical specification. So Tensor Real shape is implemented with Fin n -> Real or Array Real (not sure what is a better choice for reals), Tensor Float shape is FloatArray, but you can also have Tensor OpenCLFloat shape and get array of floats living on the GPU.
The library is designed such that you write your code polymorphic in (R Rs) [RealModel R Rs] where R is a model for real number and Rs is a type for array of Rs. To prove mathematical properties you need to assume [LawfulRealModel R Rs].

It is still quite a work in progress but I realized that using coding agents I can really nicely polish all the ideas have been working on in SciLean and thinking about for the last 5+ years. I still need a month or two of work, then I will make an announcement and write a blog post explaining all the design decisions.

Anyway, @Anatole Dedecker it might be a good idea to synchronize ti make sure your student's work is compatible with my library.

Btw if anyone is interested in how fast are different elementary linear algebra operations in Lean
https://lecopivo.github.io/NumLeanPerf/benchmarks/site/?benchmark=float-array-gemm&run=2026-06-18T053027Z&size=64&sort=mean&dir=asc&errors=1
(it is all using FloatArray I didn't bother with Array Float as I just assumed it would be terrible but maybe it I should include it :)
Array Float would be equivalent to a double** in C
Exactly, you can't ever get efficient matrix using Array Float
I started a tangent at #lean4 > Efficient value array representations @ 💬
I’d definitely coordinate with @Paul Cadman who has made an implementation of matrices based on flat Arrays for the upcoming determinant tactic :) I suspect there may be shareable work here!

Though actually, maybe I spoke too soon, since I don’t think I understand the relationship between Mathlib matrices and the current matrix work. docs#Matrix is mentioned but is in mathlib, so it’s not clear to me what API would be contributed to batteries. Is the plan to upstream Mathlib’s Matrix to batteries? Or are we discussing revamping the matrix type entirely?

François G. Dorais said:

Kim Morrison The matrix data type, basic operations and lemmas is fine for Batteries.

Anatole Dedecker Not necessarily, this is the type I think is best:

structure Matrix (m n : Nat) (a : Type _) where
  data : Array a
  get : Fin m -> Fin n -> a

Then various specialized constructors mkDense, mkSparse, mkDiag, etc.

Ugh, please, no this sort of thing should not be decided in Batteries. This needs to be decided by actually building (multiple, competing) computer algebra libraries.

Being "implementation generic" is a really bad idea, in my view. It invites designs that allow for unexpected performance pitfalls. If you're actually doing computational work, MatrixLike has no role whatsoever, and every algorithm, and every hand-off between algorithms, needs to think explicitly about representation issues.
Mathlib's Matrix is completely irrelevant in any discussion that includes the word "efficient", and should not be upstreamed anywhere.
I think if you want to show Ring (MyCustomMatrix Rat) then it would be appropriate to define the operators then use docs#Function.Injective.ring to get all the proofs, efficiency aside

Sorry, full disclosure for this conversation, I have my own DenseMatrix := Vector Vector library, with some stuff built on top of it that will be released soon (gram-schmidt + fast verified lattice basis reduction + plus more that will take longer to release). I'll be releasing 6 libraries at first, in 3 pairs, each pair having a zero-dependencies computational library and an also-depends-on-mathlib library that ties it to mathlib features.
(I don't yet have a MatrixUIntX := ByteArray wrapper, but it is on my roadmap for later.)
Is there a particular reason you chose Vector Vector instead of just Vector? It should be possible to squeeze noticeably more perf by doing that

Getting things right before going all out for performance. :-) But yes, this is another one to go for. At present I've mostly been optimizing the LLL performance, and that is arithmetic constrained, not matrix manipulation constrained, as far as I can see.
LLL in Lean would definitely make some of my dreams come true!

Kim Morrison said:

Being "implementation generic" is a really bad idea, in my view. It invites designs that allow for unexpected performance pitfalls.

(+1, for the same reason that we have both Array and List and different API between the two! :) )

By the way, Kim, are your libraries (I’m guessing) more focused on verified algorithms that are efficient when compiled, or do they also cover things like “efficiently produce a meta-level proof that a given operation on some symbolic matrix normalizes to such-and-such”? (I’m curious here both about kernel reduction for the literal case and the more general symbolic case)

Kim Morrison said:

Getting things right before going all out for performance. :-) But yes, this is another one to go for. At present I've mostly been optimizing the LLL performance, and that is arithmetic constrained, not matrix manipulation constrained, as far as I can see.

Seems like people on the internet haven't done much roofline analysis for LLL to back up or refute that claim :(
@Henrik Böving, could you explain that last comment? It sounds very interesting but I don't understand yet what you're saying.

Yes.

Thomas Murrills said:

I’d definitely coordinate with Paul Cadman who has made an implementation of matrices based on flat Arrays for the upcoming determinant tactic :) I suspect there may be shareable work here!

I'm not proposing to add a different implementation of Matrix to Mathlib as part of the determinant tactic work. The determinant tactic will work with the existing Mathlib matrix definition. Mathlib's matrix notation is a performance bottleneck - so I may propose a more efficient elaboration for matrix notation that uses Arrays.

Kim Morrison said:

Henrik Böving, could you explain that last comment? It sounds very interesting but I don't understand yet what you're saying.

In HPC you can do several analyses to figure out if an algorithm is indeed computation or memory bound. The easiest metric for this is the so called "operational intensity" which is in essence #flops/#non-cheap-memory accesses. There are also more sophisticated analyses you can do such as roofline ones.

You can for example show that Matrix x Vector multiplication has a very low (and constant) operational intensity so it is basically useless to spend much time optimizing the computation because the amount of memory you have to consume to make the computation bottlenecks you, not the computation itself. You can also show that Matrix x Matrix has an intensity of O(n) so there is actually potential in squeezing the CPU harder because you are guaranteed not to be memory bound etc. (That said, the naive matrix x matrix algorithm is in fact of similar operational intensity to matrix x vector and you need to use cool tricks like tiling to actually get benefits)
